children: By Mike Cherney | Photography by Kathy Anne Lim for WSJ

SINGAPORE-As the equivalent of a deputy minister for defense, Desmond Choo helps oversee this city-state's military in a tough geopolitical neighborhood. This year he's taken on another fight: Defending constituents against swarms of cicadas never before seen here.

"When the cicada surges escalate to a point where it starts to significantly disrupt home life across a neighborhood, we had to act decisively," said Choo, who represents the hardest-hit area in Singapore's parliament.

Built on a jungle island roughly 85 miles north of the equator, Singapore is no stranger to cicadas. Until recently, there were 10 known species living there. But residents were perplexed when tens of thousands appeared, annoying locals with their loud songs and haphazard flying.

Scientists determined they were orange-winged cicadas that had previously been found in the Philippines. How the critters, which move in larger swarms than Singapore's other cicada species, got to the island is unknown.

They were "all over the corridor, the floors, the wall," said Ashukumar Veerappan, 65, a resident of a housing complex that was menaced by the intruders. "They hit on your face and everywhere. They just fly blindly."

During the peak of the chaos, Veerappan heard screams every night from neighbors. Parents said cicadas banging into windows prevented their children from sleeping. Residents used shawls and umbrellas to protect themselves in open-air hallways.

Some began griping to local media and the authorities sprang into action-with a hallmark efficiency that has helped Singapore transform from a struggling postcolonial trading post to a modern financial hub.

A "Cicada Management Taskforce," led by Choo and comprising scientists, community groups and the national parks agency, wrapped foil or plastic around more than 500 trees and laid coconut husk mats or tarpaulin at their base. They hoped to disrupt the molting process of cicada nymphs, which need to shed their outer layer to emerge as adults.

In government-subsidized apartment buildings, where most Singaporeans live, some ceiling lights were masked to see if cicadas would be less attracted to them. Municipal workers roamed the hallways with nets. Light traps, made from sheets, lamps and containers of soapy water, were used to corner the bugs.

"Because cicada surges are not well-studied in dense tropical urban settings, no single agency had an off-the-shelf solution," said Choo, a member of the People's Action Party that has governed Singapore since 1959.

Singapore isn't used to half measures. Chewing gum is effectively banned and some criminals are still caned. But the streets are clean, multinational companies are here in droves and the island country frequently ranks at the top of livability indexes.
Due to that success, expectations are high for a perfectly functioning and harmonious society.
"If Singapore has a national pastime beyond lining up for food and scoring deals, it is complaining," read a 2024 article in the Straits Times that dubbed it "complain nation."

It has been an effective recipe. "They do look into it when more people start to complain," Veerappan said. He is on the executive committee of the opposition Singapore Democratic Party, which hasn't had a member of parliament since the 1990s, but said he was "quite satisfied" with the government's cicada effort.

The U.S., where there are both annual and periodical cicada swarms, tends to take a more laissez-faire approach. The Environmental Protection Agency says the bugs, which are largely harmless, will leave eventually.

Carlos Kennerley, who lives in the same building as Veerappan, said when his 29-year-old daughter, Aisyah, came home from work, she would call him to meet her at the elevator-with a badminton racket in hand.
"You stand outside and your ears are ringing," said Kennerley, 59, a Brit who has lived in Singapore for decades. "You come into a quiet place and it's like, 'Whoa.'"

Foo Maosheng, an entomologist at the National University of Singapore's Lee Kong Chian Natural History Museum, usually specializes in cockroaches. Nonetheless, he deployed to the front lines of the cicada invasion, which runs from about March to June.

Whether it is a health or economic problem, Singaporeans "tend to have this concept of creating a working group in order to handle the situation," said Foo, who was on the task force and provided input on cicada biology. "It's very similar to back in the Covid times."
Over three nights, Foo said he caught 1,733 cicadas using the light traps. Many are now stored in his lab at the museum; he's also got 1,363 moltings in a jar.
Local officials said 22,000 cicadas were captured this year, that residents reported less noise and that the situation appeared to stabilize.

How that affects next year is uncertain. Foo said he doesn't know how many years the orange-winged cicadas need to spend underground-he estimated between two and six-meaning next year's bugs may be the offspring of adults from several years prior.
The tree wrappings and light traps worked well, Choo said. The goal was to reduce the impacts on residents, not totally eradicate the cicadas.
For next year, officials are exploring using very targeted pesticides and will prune trees early to remove potential egg-laying sites.
"We moved away from broad guesswork," Choo said. "We now have a clearer, better-tested playbook."
